title: CREATING A PSYCHOLOGICALLY SUPPORTIVE ENVIRONMENT THROUGH AURAL ARCHITECTURE
research_question: How can aural architecture create a psychologically supportive environment by applying the Reasonable Person Model (RPM) to understand its role in perception, model-building, attention, and preference?

findings.antecedent: Aural architecture (integrating physical, perceptual, and cultural aspects of sound)
findings.consequent: High-quality acoustic environment that responds to human needs and enhances well-being
findings.mechanism: Aural architecture, when designed to align with human information-processing, supports psychological well-being.
findings.quote: aural architecture is to provide a high-quality acoustic environment which responds to human needs and enhances their well-being.

findings.antecedent: Sound reflections from different architectural shapes, materials, and volumes
findings.consequent: Understanding of the environment and generation of a mental map of the place
findings.mechanism: Sound reflections contribute to creating a soundscape that provides cues for spatial perception and cognitive mapping, aligning with the model-building domain of RPM.
findings.quote: sound reflections from different shapes, materials and volumes of architectural spaces plays a significant role in creating a soundscape that contribute to understanding the environment and generating a mental map of the place

findings.antecedent: Sounds created by reflections acting as sensory stimuli
findings.mechanism: Sensory stimuli from reflections can lead to attention-fatigue, reducing human effectiveness, as per the effectiveness domain of RPM.
findings.quote: sounds created by these reflections act as a sensory stimulus, which affect human effectiveness by resulting in attention-fatigue

findings.antecedent: Acoustic aesthetics
findings.mechanism: Acoustic aesthetics can act as an involuntary fascination, allowing for attention restoration, aligning with the effectiveness domain of RPM.
findings.quote: acoustic aesthetics can act as an involuntary fascination that allows for attention restoration

findings.antecedent: Preferred aural architectural design (applying preference-matrix model)
findings.mechanism: Designing environments based on preference (coherence, legibility, complexity, mystery) leads to a supportive environment, fulfilling the meaningful actions domain of RPM.
findings.quote: creating a preferred aural architectural design through applying the preference-matrix model can lead to a supportive environment.

findings.antecedent: Lack of definiteness due to echo
findings.consequent: Speech understanding in activities requiring directed attention (e.g., attending a lecture)
findings.mechanism: Echo minimizes definiteness, disturbing speech understanding and maximizing the use of directed attention, negatively affecting place users.
findings.quote: the lack of definiteness due to echo might disturb speech understanding in other activities such as attending a lecture which will maximize the use of directed attention

findings.antecedent: Rapid change in environment (e.g., rollercoaster in dark, enclosed space)
findings.consequent: Perception of environment (e.g., localizing sound source, sense of location)
findings.mechanism: Rapid change negatively affects perception, making it difficult to localize sound sources or get a sense of location.
findings.quote: if we consider being on a rollercoaster in a dark, enclosed space... it would be extremely difficult to localize the sound speaker—or even get a sense of our location

findings.antecedent: Sound diffusers
findings.mechanism: Sound diffusers provide homogenous spatial and temporal reflections, making it difficult to localize the sound source.
findings.quote: sound diffusers tend to cause difficulty in localizing the sound source because they provide a homogenous special and temporal reflections

findings.antecedent: Auditory illusion
findings.mechanism: Auditory illusion influences mental map creation and requires more directed attention, potentially leading to attention-fatigue.
findings.quote: the auditory illusion influences the process of mental map creation, and requires more directed attention.

findings.antecedent: Complex auditory scenes (especially when difficult to distinguish sound events)
findings.mechanism: Complexity in auditory scenes, particularly when sound events are indistinguishable, demands more directed attention.
findings.quote: complex auditory scenes could require more attention [10] because of the complexity being possibly resulted by being in multiple acoustic arenas

findings.antecedent: Highly diffusive and absorptive places (e.g., acoustic chambers)
findings.mechanism: Such environments make it difficult to define the original direction of the sound source, leading to a loss of spatial awareness.
findings.quote: creating highly diffusive and absorptive places, such as the acoustic champers, results in losing sense of space.

findings.antecedent: Extremely high homogeneity in reverberation from different directions
findings.mechanism: Lack of clear directional cues from reverberation can create a disorienting sensation.
findings.quote: extremely high homogeneity in the reverberation from different directions create the sensation of flying

findings.antecedent: Overusing directed attention for long periods without rest or involuntary fascination
findings.consequent: Ability to remain focused, tendency to make unreasonable decisions, difficulty in productivity
findings.mechanism: Overuse of directed attention leads to attention-fatigue, impairing cognitive functions and productivity.
findings.quote: overusing directed attention for long periods of time without taking a rest or using involuntary fascination to restore it will most likely result in the inability to remain focused, the tendency to make unreasonable decisions, and promote difficulty in productivity

findings.antecedent: Spaces that enhance the ability to locate sound source
findings.mechanism: Minimizing the use of directed attention by making sound sources easily localizable helps prevent attention-fatigue.
findings.quote: minimizing the use of directed attention, architects can hence create a space that enhances the ability to locate sound source.

findings.antecedent: Aesthetics (e.g., listening to sound with special characteristics in an ideal room)
findings.mechanism: Aesthetics can be a source of involuntary fascination, which allows for attention restoration.
findings.quote: Attention restoration can be achieved by being exposed to involuntary fascination [11], a considered source of which are aesthetics [2].

findings.antecedent: Environmental features that contribute to feeling comfortable (Kaplan's preference-matrix: coherence, legibility, complexity, mystery)
findings.consequent: Preferred environments (supporting information processing, enhancing health and effectiveness)
findings.mechanism: Preferred environments are based on universal features that facilitate understanding and exploration, minimizing directed attention and fostering involuntary fascination.
findings.quote: Kaplans' preference-matrix model of environmental preference suggests that the highly-preferred environments are the ones which are easy to understand and allow for more exploration

findings.antecedent: Coherence (pattern recognition, sound grouping, identifying objects, distinguishing from background, musical ratios in architecture)
findings.mechanism: Coherence, linked to pattern recognition and sound grouping, helps make sense of the auditory environment.
findings.quote: First, coherence is linked to pattern recognition, such as spectral balance, decay rate, initial delay and onset shape. Additionally, it is related to sound grouping and identifying objects

findings.antecedent: Legibility (spatial sound cues, temporal aspects of sound behavior, listener location relative to sound source)
findings.consequent: Navigation of space and formation of cognitive map
findings.mechanism: Legibility, through clear spatial sound cues, aids in navigating and understanding the environment.
findings.quote: legibility is connected to navigating a space through spatial sound cues

findings.antecedent: Complexity (diversity of sound elements, balance of reflection/absorption/diffusion, multiple auditory scenes, background sound)
findings.mechanism: A balanced level of complexity provides sufficient information to encourage exploration without overwhelming the cognitive system.
findings.quote: complexity depends on the diversity of sound elements and can be achieved by creating a balance between sound reflection, absorption and diffusion

findings.antecedent: Complexity (if not coherent)
findings.mechanism: Incoherent complex sounds can create a negative effect and make perception more difficult.
findings.quote: this negative effect may occur only if complex sounds are not coherent [1].

findings.antecedent: Mystery (hiding part of information, creating interest, e.g., whispering galleries, large domes creating 'acousmêtre' effect, echoes/reverberation in worship spaces)
findings.mechanism: Mystery creates an interest in thinking about the environment, fostering involuntary fascination and exploration.
findings.quote: by hiding part of information and creating an interest of thinking about it, mystery is achieved.

findings.antecedent: Failure to create preferred environments
findings.mechanism: Environments that do not support information processing and well-being lead to cognitive and physiological stress.
findings.quote: The failure of creating preferred environments creates stress, which can be responsible for attention fatigue, and therefore reducing productivity.

findings.antecedent: Lack of privacy (uncontrollable and/or unpredictable sounds)
findings.consequent: Stress (due to sounds affecting cognitive activities)
findings.mechanism: Uncontrollable and unpredictable sounds, especially in the absence of privacy, increase stress and attention fatigue.
findings.quote: The stress can even increase with the lack of privacy, the reason being sounds affect cognitive activities, especially if uncontrollable and/or unpredictable [1].

findings.antecedent: Architectural elements (determining boundaries of acoustic events)
findings.mechanism: If architectural elements fail to define acoustic boundaries appropriate for different activities (e.g., focus vs. communication), productivity can be negatively affected.
findings.quote: if these elements fail to do so, humans' productivity can be affected.

findings.antecedent: Low predictability of the aural environment (e.g., coffee shop vs. friend's home)
findings.mechanism: Low predictability in public spaces makes it difficult to predict aural events, leading to attention-fatigue and reduced focus.
findings.quote: in the second case (the coffee shop), because it is a public space, it is difficult to predict the aural environment... this environment is considered un-preferred as it can lead to attention-fatigue.

mechanisms: The Reasonable Person Model (RPM) provides a framework to understand how humans interact with environments through three domains: model-building (creating mental maps), effectiveness (managing attention and fatigue), and meaningful actions (achieving supportive environments based on preference).
Aural architecture influences model-building by providing sound cues (reflections, soundscapes) that contribute to understanding the environment and forming cognitive maps.
Aural architecture influences effectiveness by modulating directed attention fatigue and promoting attention restoration through involuntary fascination (e.g., acoustic aesthetics).

Aural architecture influences meaningful actions by creating preferred environments based on Kaplan's preference-matrix (coherence, legibility, complexity, mystery), which support information processing and well-being.
Lack of control and predictability in the acoustic environment leads to stress and attention fatigue.
moderators: Familiarity (influences individual preference based on universal features)
Cultural background (influences sound preference and perception)
Activity type (different activities have different acoustic requirements)
implementation_implications: Architects should design aural environments to enhance perception and model-building, reduce directed attention, and align with preference models.
Design should consider sound reflections, materials, and volumes to create coherent and legible soundscapes for spatial understanding.
Acoustic aesthetics should be leveraged to create involuntary fascination for attention restoration.
Design for coherence, legibility, complexity, and mystery in aural environments to create psychologically supportive spaces.
Provide acoustic privacy and predictability to minimize stress and attention fatigue, especially in task-oriented environments.

tables.description: Kaplans' preference-matrix, showing how coherence and legibility contribute to understanding, and complexity and mystery contribute to exploration.

limitations: The paper does not present new empirical data but synthesizes existing literature to apply a theoretical model. Therefore, it does not have traditional limitations related to study design, sample size, or statistical power.
